fields.description: Biblical leadership looks nothing like the world's. Here is what makes a godly leader — servanthood, humility, character, and dependence on God — drawn from Scripture and the great pastoral classics.
fields.body_html:
The world has a clear picture of a leader: someone at the top, in command, whose word decides and whose position is served by those beneath. When the disciples argued about who was the greatest, they were simply assuming that picture. And Jesus overturned it completely. “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them,” he said, “and their great ones exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant” (Matthew 20:25–26). In one sentence he turned leadership upside down — or rather, right side up. Godly leadership is not less than the world’s idea of leadership; it is something altogether different in kind. Here is what marks it.

It leads by serving

The first and deepest mark of a godly leader is that he leads by serving. This is not a technique or a softer management style; it is the very shape of Christ’s own leadership. “The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28). On the last night before the cross, the Lord of glory took a towel and washed his disciples’ feet, then said, “I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you” (John 13:15). A godly leader, then, is not measured by how many serve him but by how truly he serves. He asks not “How can these people advance my vision?” but “How can I lay down my life for their good?” The higher the office, the lower he stoops.

It is rooted in humility

Beneath servanthood lies humility, and without it every other qualification curdles. Andrew Murray, in his searching little book Humility, called it the root of every grace, and warned that pride is the one sin most fatal to those who lead in the church. He wrote that humility is not one virtue among many but the soil in which all the others grow:

Humility is the only soil in which the graces root; the lack of humility is the sufficient explanation of every defect and failure.Andrew Murray, Humility

Scripture agrees without qualification: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5). A leader who forgets this sets himself against the very grace he needs. But the humble leader — who knows that any gift he has is received, that he is a servant and not a lord, that he stands only by mercy — is exactly the kind of person God delights to use and to bless. “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23:12); the way up, in God’s kingdom, is always down.

It rests on character, not charisma

When Scripture describes the leaders of the church, it dwells overwhelmingly on character rather than charisma. An elder must be “above reproach… sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable… not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money” (1 Timothy 3:2–3). Peter tells the shepherds of the flock to lead “not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3). The godly leader leads chiefly by what he is. Richard Baxter built his whole classic The Reformed Pastor on this principle, charging ministers first of all to “take heed to yourselves” before taking heed to the flock, because a leader’s life either lends weight to his words or empties them. People are shaped far more by what they see in their leaders than by what they hear from them. A gifted, magnetic leader with a hollow character will, in the end, do the flock harm; a leader of quiet, tested integrity will do them lasting good, whether or not he dazzles.

It depends on God, not on itself

The godly leader knows he cannot do the work in his own strength, and so he leads on his knees. He has taken to heart Jesus’ words, “apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), and he believes them enough to pray. E. M. Bounds, in Power Through Prayer, insisted that the power of a spiritual leader is not in his methods or abilities but in the God he depends on — that leaders are made in the secret place of prayer before they are ever seen in public. The leader who prays little, however busy and capable, is leading in his own strength; the leader who prays much is drawing on a strength not his own. This is why Scripture pairs the ministry of the word with prayer as the two things the church’s leaders must give themselves to: “we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word” (Acts 6:4). A godly leader guards his communion with God as the source of everything else.

It seeks the good of the led, not the leader

Finally, the godly leader exists for the sake of those he leads, not the other way round. The false leader uses the flock; the true leader feeds it. God’s anger burned against the shepherds of Israel precisely because they had it backwards: “Should not shepherds feed the sheep? … The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed” (Ezekiel 34:2–4). By contrast the Good Shepherd “lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). A godly leader measures success not by his own advancement but by the flourishing of those in his care — are they growing, being fed, drawing nearer to God? He is willing to decrease so that they and their Lord may increase, saying with John the Baptist, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

It is faithful in what is small

One more mark deserves mention, because Scripture makes so much of it and we make so little: the godly leader is proven in small and hidden things before he is trusted with large and public ones. Jesus laid down the principle: “One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much” (Luke 16:10). God’s ordinary way is to test a person’s faithfulness in obscurity — in the unseen duties, the unglamorous service, the promises kept when no one is watching — and only then to enlarge their trust. David kept his father’s sheep before he shepherded a nation; the faithful servants in Jesus’ parable were told, “You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much” (Matthew 25:21). This guards us against two errors at once. It warns the impatient, who want influence before they have proved faithful, that God’s school of leadership is long and begins low. And it encourages the overlooked, laboring away in some small and thankless place, that nothing done faithfully for God is wasted — that this very hiddenness may be the training ground in which he is quietly forming a leader. The person who despises the day of small things is not ready to lead; the person who serves gladly in them is being made ready.

The pattern and the power

Put these marks together and a portrait emerges that looks nothing like the world’s idea of a great leader and everything like Jesus: a servant, humble, of proven character, dependent on God, spending himself for the good of others. That is not an accident. Christian leadership is simply Christ-likeness given responsibility; it is following the Shepherd closely enough that others can safely follow you. This is deeply freeing, because it means godly leadership is not reserved for the naturally commanding or charismatic. It is open to anyone willing to take the lowest place, to serve, to grow in humility and character, and to lean hard on God. “Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5, KJV) — the mind that, being in the form of God, took the form of a servant. Wherever that mind is formed in a person and given a trust, there you will find a leader worth following, because through them people are being led not merely to a goal or a vision, but to Christ himself.

And there is great hope in this for anyone who feels their own unfitness. The leaders God has used most were rarely the most impressive by human reckoning; they were men and women who knew their weakness and therefore clung to God. Moses protested that he could not speak; Gideon called himself the least in his family; Paul came “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3). God was not hindered by their weakness — he was glorified through it, so that the power might plainly be his and not theirs. If you are called to lead in any sphere — a church, a home, a team, a mission — do not wait until you feel strong and adequate. Come as you are, humble and dependent, take up the towel, and follow the Servant-King. He makes godly leaders out of ordinary, willing people, and he has never yet run short of grace for the task.
